subject: READING
prompt: What did Ebbinghaus memorize for his experiments?
passage: In 1885, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus set out to measure something that seemed unmeasurable: forgetting. Using himself as the only subject, he memorized lists of meaningless syllables and then tested his recall after various intervals. His results traced a steep downward slope now known as the forgetting curve. Within an hour, he had lost more than half of what he had learned; after a day, roughly two-thirds was gone. After that, the losses slowed, and a small remainder persisted for weeks. Ebbinghaus's more hopeful discovery concerned how forgetting can be resisted. Each time he reviewed a list, the curve flattened, and the material took longer to fade. Reviews spread out over several days proved far more effective than the same amount of study crammed into a single session, a principle now called spaced repetition. Modern research has repeatedly confirmed this finding. The implication for students is uncomfortable but clear: the all-night cram session before an exam may produce a passing grade the next morning, but it builds knowledge on sand.
choices: lines of poetry
lists of meaningless syllables
names of his students
long strings of numbers
explanation: The passage says 'he memorized lists of meaningless syllables and then tested his recall.'

subject: READING
prompt: What did Tomas have to bring up from the bottom of the pool?
passage: The whistle shrieked, and Tomas dove. For three summers he had watched the lifeguards from his towel, envying their red suits and their easy authority, and now the only thing between him and that tall white chair was a ten-pound brick at the bottom of the deep end. He kicked downward. The water pressed against his ears, and the brick, when his fingers finally closed around it, seemed bolted to the tiles. His lungs began their familiar protest. Last year, at exactly this moment, he had let go and surfaced empty-handed, and he had spent the following twelve months telling everyone that he had not really wanted the job anyway. He thought of that lie now, how it had tasted worse than chlorine. He planted his feet against the bottom, hugged the brick to his chest, and pushed. When he broke the surface, gasping, the instructor glanced at her stopwatch and said nothing at all. She simply nodded toward the shelf where the red suits were folded.
choices: a ten-pound brick
a whistle
a red suit
a stopwatch
explanation: The passage says the only thing between him and the lifeguard chair 'was a ten-pound brick at the bottom of the deep end.'

subject: READING
prompt: According to the passage, why is the diner still open?
passage: The Harlow textile mill had once employed half the town. Now its windows stared out like hollow eyes, every pane shattered or missing. The diner still operated, but only because old Mr. Petersen refused to retire, even though most afternoons he served more coffee to the walls than to customers.
choices: It is always crowded with customers
The mill has reopened
Mr. Petersen refuses to retire
It is the newest business on Main Street
explanation: The passage says the diner operated 'only because old Mr. Petersen refused to retire.'

subject: READING
prompt: How does the extended metaphor of a chess game develop the passage's central idea?
passage: Negotiations between the two nations had become a chess game played in slow motion. Each diplomatic note was a pawn pushed forward with calculated precision, testing the opponent's response. The trade embargo was a bishop cutting diagonally across the board, threatening positions that seemed secure. When the smaller nation unexpectedly formed an alliance with a neighboring power, it was a knight's move -- surprising, indirect, and suddenly putting the larger nation's king in check. The diplomats on both sides understood that in this game, there were no spare pieces. Every move spent a resource that could not be recovered.
choices: It suggests that diplomacy is a trivial game that politicians play for fun
It implies that one nation is clearly winning and the other is losing
It shows that diplomacy involves calculated moves, each of which carries a permanent cost
It shows that diplomacy follows predictable, rule-based patterns that lead to guaranteed outcomes
correctAnswer: It shows that diplomacy involves calculated moves, each of which carries a permanent cost
explanation: Each diplomatic act is a deliberate chess move, and the passage ends, 'Every move spent a resource that could not be recovered,' stressing lasting consequences.
